title: A general decoder for T-cell antigen recognition

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable way to predict what a T cell recognizes from its T-cell receptor, a candidate peptide antigen and the molecule presenting that peptide. In the supplied conceptual framework, recognition concerns a peptide presented by a particular major histocompatibility complex molecule, rather than a peptide considered alone. A general decoder would work across unfamiliar receptors, peptides and presentation molecules, including targets that have not already been studied experimentally. This is a proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

The intended scope includes several distinct outputs: predicting receptor binding, predicting the functional response of a cell and identifying cells relevant to disease. These require separate validation. The framework also allows a receptor to recognize multiple targets through cross-reactivity, so decoding recognition need not produce one unique antigen per receptor. Binding alone would not establish whether a cell produces a particular response. These scientific distinctions are retained from the supplied research and review, whose accessible source material did not independently substantiate them.

significance.text: Conditional on reliable generalization, the direct advance would be the ability to propose previously untested recognition relationships and prioritize experiments around them. Researchers could move from extensive searches toward more targeted screening, with predictions that can be tested. This could reduce some experimental search, but the supplied evidence does not establish how much screening could be replaced or how often predictions would succeed in practice.

As a conditional synthesis, this capability could accelerate infection, cancer and autoimmunity research by helping connect T cells with candidate targets. Its practical value would depend on which output is reliable: a binding predictor could guide target discovery, while a validated functional predictor could support a broader set of experimental decisions. Neither output alone would establish disease relevance, treatment benefit or clinical safety. Identifying disease-relevant cells and supporting clinical decisions would require additional evidence in independent patient populations.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability, as framed by the supplied materials, is dependable prediction beyond familiar examples across the joint space of receptors, peptides and presentation molecules. A decoder must capture recognition relationships well enough to handle unfamiliar components and natural variants. Its evaluation must distinguish genuinely new components from new combinations of components already represented in development data; otherwise, apparent generalization could address a narrower problem than the innovation requires.

The concrete barriers implied by this framework include representing the presentation context, accommodating cross-reactivity and connecting predicted binding to a specified cellular response. A single binding score cannot by itself demonstrate all three capabilities. Functional prediction needs explicitly defined response endpoints, and disease-cell identification needs an operational definition of relevance. The supplied review identifies these as distinctions that an eventual system and its evaluation must preserve, rather than capabilities already demonstrated.

A further engineering barrier is making predictions useful when true binders are rare. As an evaluation synthesis, a system must provide confidence estimates that remain informative in that setting and must expose the consequences of false positive and false negative predictions. Performance on a selected set of examples would not by itself establish usefulness for a much broader experimental search. The supplied materials propose testing calibration under rare-binder prevalence but do not provide an established numerical target.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a benchmark to Lu et al., titled “Assessment of computational methods in predicting TCR–epitope binding recognition,” with an online publication date of 28 November 2025 and DOI 10.1038/s41592-025-02910-0. It describes an evaluation of 50 models and reports difficulty across the tested models in generalizing to unseen epitopes. These bibliographic details, the model count and the reported finding remain unverified within the supplied review: its retained copy of the intended PubMed page contained only a cookie-access notice, without article metadata or scientific text.

The source index records a saved HTML artifact retrieved on 11 November 2026, with 153 extracted characters and no recorded truncation or extraction issues. Those file-level properties do not establish that an article or abstract was captured. According to the supplied review, the retained content did not confirm the intended paper's identity or support assessment of its methods and results. This access limitation leaves the attributed benchmark unresolved; it is not evidence that the paper or its reported result is false.

Even if the attributed benchmark details are confirmed, an evaluation of 50 models would describe the tested methods and conditions, rather than every possible method. A binding-recognition benchmark would also not establish functional-response prediction or prospective identification of disease-relevant cells. No usable scientific text in the supplied evidence establishes demonstrated performance for those broader capabilities.

The supplied freshness record is empty, leaving subsequent developments through 1 November 2026 unassessed. The later artifact retrieval date does not resolve that gap. The materials therefore support retaining the innovation as an open research objective, while leaving both the cited benchmark's particulars and the broader contemporary performance landscape unsettled.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct blinded tests across multiple laboratories using diverse receptors, peptide–presentation molecule combinations and natural variants. Specify in advance which receptors, peptides, presentation molecules and combinations are held unseen, and report results separately for those forms of novelty. This would make the demonstrated scope of generalization explicit. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not documented consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: measure binding and predefined functional responses independently, with reproducible experimental procedures and disclosed evaluation methods. Show how prediction confidence corresponds to observed outcomes when true binders are rare, and report error rates at operating points relevant to the intended screening task. Useful calibration and acceptable error rates must be defined for that task; the supplied materials establish no universal numerical threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: prospectively identify disease-relevant cells in independent patient cohorts, using a prespecified definition of disease relevance and validation beyond a binding prediction alone. Reproduction across laboratories and cohorts would strengthen the case for practical utility. Clinical applications would still need application-specific validation. Finite tests could establish breadth across the tested receptors, antigens, presentation contexts and endpoints, but could not prove literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: IMM-02, “A predictive, causal theory of whole immune responses,” has a broader target. A recognition decoder could supply information about one class of interactions, while a whole-response theory would need to explain how interactions combine into system-level outcomes. IMM-01's separate treatment of binding and cellular function already marks a boundary between recognizing a target and predicting the resulting immune response.

Roster-based synthesis: IMM-03, “Vaccine design that reliably directs broadly protective antibody evolution,” concerns directing antibody development, whereas IMM-01 concerns decoding T-cell recognition. IMM-04, “Durable, antigen-specific reversal of established autoimmunity,” and IMM-05, “Routine donor-specific transplant tolerance without lifelong immunosuppression,” could benefit from identifying relevant recognition relationships, but each requires a durable therapeutic change that decoding alone would not demonstrate.

Roster-based synthesis: IMM-06, “General immune eradication of heterogeneous solid tumors,” and IMM-07, “Immune-mediated, treatment-free control of established HIV infection,” share an interest in disease-relevant immune targets. A decoder could help prioritize candidate targets or cells for investigation. Tumor eradication and sustained HIV control remain separate outcome-level achievements, requiring evidence beyond target recognition or a predicted cell response.

Roster-based synthesis: IMM-08, “Restoration of youthful immune competence in older adults,” addresses broad immune performance. IMM-09, “In-body programming of immune cells as an inexpensive, scalable treatment,” addresses the ability to alter cells therapeutically. Recognition predictions might inform assessment or programming choices, but they would not establish restored competence, successful in-body programming, affordability or scalability.

Roster-based synthesis: IMM-10, “Real-time immune control of life-threatening systemic inflammation,” focuses on controlling a changing systemic response. IMM-11, “Causal mechanisms that initiate the breakdown of self-tolerance,” focuses on explaining disease initiation. A decoder could contribute recognition-level information to either investigation, but predicting a recognition relationship would not itself establish a control strategy or identify the causal event that initiated loss of tolerance.

Roster-based synthesis: IMM-12, “Programmable trained immunity with predictable protection and safety,” IMM-13, “Predictive causal control of microbiome–immune interactions,” and IMM-14, “Causal, bidirectional control of neuroimmune circuits,” concern additional forms of immune programming and interaction. Their overlap with IMM-01 is the broader ambition of making immune behavior predictable. Each retains a distinct causal or intervention goal that a T-cell recognition decoder would not by itself fulfill.

change_log.reason: The research and review distinguish these capabilities and require separate validation; consolidating them into one prediction claim would overstate the innovation.

unresolved_issues: The intended paper's identity, publication date, DOI, model count and reported generalization result require confirmation from accessible scientific content.

The supplied retained source does not independently substantiate the conceptual background concerning presentation specificity, cross-reactivity or the relationship between binding and cellular response.
Developments through 1 November 2026 remain unassessed; the supplied materials do not establish the latest performance of binding or functional-response predictors.

An operational evaluation must define held-unseen components and combinations, functional endpoints, natural-variant coverage, relevant rare-binder prevalence, useful calibration and disease relevance.
The amount of experimental search that a successful decoder could save, and its eventual clinical utility, remain unquantified.
